newsitem.title: ITALY: Brembo target price seen at 15-16,000 lire.
newsitem.headline: Brembo target price seen at 15-16,000 lire.

text.p: Italian automotive brake maker Brembo, after announcing 1996 results below expectations, should have a share target price of around 15-16,000 lire, analysts said.
Brembo remains suspended limit down on the Milan bourse with a theoretical price of 16,950 lire against a pre-opening price of 19,650 lire on Monday.
The company last week announced 1996 consolidated net profit of 19.1 billion lire against 30.1 billion previously although turnover rose to 357.4 billion from 331.2 billion.

It said consolidated earnings before interest and tax equalled 9.8 percent of turnover against 14.3 percent in 1995. It said the results were below expectations and forecast a 1997 margin of 10.5 percent.

"After the sharp fall in profit levels Brembo is still a very interesting company but the stock is too dear," said Antonio Antonio Tognoli, analyst at ING Bank which considers a correct price of between 15,000 and 16,000 lire.
Tognoli had expected a 1996 margin of 12.5 percent and forecasts 1997 turnover rising by 15 percent with a margin of 10.3 percent increasing to 14.5 percent in 1999.
Brokers Milla Sim, immediately after Brembo announced its 1996 results, confirmed its Sell recommendation on the company and set a target price of 15,000 lire.
Monte Paschi Mercato Sim put a Reduce on the stock "with a target certainly below 17,000 lire," said analyst Simona Pedrazzini.
For AFV Sim the right price was around 15,000 lire. "We have revised down 1997 forecasts seeing net profit of 23 billion lire against 37 billion," said analyst Ilario Presta.

"It was clear that a shift towards lower end of the market areas, like brakes for scooters and production for the U.S. market, as well as the lira's appreciation, would have led to lower margins," said Gianluca Pediconi of Milla.
"We haven't yet made a complete evaluation of the company's prospects, but there will certainly be a revision downwards of forecasts in the order of 30 percent," he said.
